Today it is only ever consumed inside a permutation test (scripts/detection_floor_table.py:76-83), which calibrates it, so no wrong number is currently produced - this is a trap set for S2, where MASTER-PLAN says 'Also compute glm_contrast_z. Report both.'
findings.evidence: Measured null distribution of glm_contrast_z with V=58 (the FFCr parcel size), na=nb=15, equicorrelated Gaussian vertices, 4000 replicates per point, true means identical: rho=0.00 -> null SD 0.136, P(|stat|>1.96)=0.0000; rho=0.20 -> 0.483, 0.0000; rho=0.50 -> 0.748, 0.0092; rho=0.80 -> 0.944, 0.0355; rho=0.95 -> 1.029, 0.0520; rho=1.00 -> 1.057, 0.0617. The false-positive rate of a 1.96 threshold thus swings from 0.0000 to 0.062 with rho alone. Null mean stays at 0.00 throughout, so the statistic is unbiased - it is only the scale that is undefined. (Note the accompanying negative result: this is NOT a power pathology. For a uniform effect, mean-of-t and t-of-ROI-mean have identical SNR to first order, both delta*sqrt(n/2)/(sigma*sqrt(rho+(1-rho)/V)), and mean-of-t is better under heteroscedastic per-vertex noise. The brief's 'known pathology when vertices are strongly correlated' is real but is purely about calibration, not sensitivity.)
findings.concrete_failure: S2 reports glm_contrast_z for FFC-right, PPA, EBA, VWFA and V1 and compares the values to Meta's Fig 4 z-map, or applies a z>1.96 / z>3.1 threshold. With realistic TRIBE prediction correlation the ROI statistic's null width is well under 1, so every ROI reads as sub-threshold and the paper concludes 'no category selectivity survives correction' when the permutation test on the same numbers would have rejected. Conversely if a reader assumes null SD 1 and rho happens to be near 1, the nominal 5% is really 6.2%.
findings.fix: Rename to make the scale explicit (e.g. glm_contrast_meant or roi_mean_t) or, better, return the ROI-level studentised statistic instead of the mean of per-vertex ones. At minimum add a hard warning to the docstring: 'The returned value is a mean of per-vertex t-statistics. Its null SD is approximately sqrt(rho_bar) and is NOT 1. It must be calibrated by permutation; never threshold it at a normal quantile and never compare it numerically to a published per-vertex z-map.' Pin the measured null SDs above in a test so the property cannot be forgotten.

findings.title: glm_contrast_z silently scores non-finite and perfectly-separating vertices as z = 0, attenuating the ROI statistic toward the null with no warning
findings.claim: The mask `ok = se > 0` is False for NaN (NaN > 0 evaluates False without warning), so any vertex with non-finite data contributes exactly 0 to the ROI mean instead of propagating NaN or raising. The same line also maps the opposite extreme to 0: a vertex that is constant within each condition but differs between them (se = 0, diff != 0) is infinitely significant and is scored as null. Both directions bias the ROI statistic toward zero, i.e. toward a NO-GO, and both are completely silent - no warning, no error, no NaN in the output.
findings.evidence: Lines 341-344: `z = np.zeros_like(diff)` / `ok = se > 0` / `z[ok] = diff[ok] / se[ok]` / `return float(z.mean())`. Run with warnings.simplefilter('error') to prove silence: a 5-vertex ROI where vertex 2 is all-NaN in condition A returns 17.7924 with no warning and no error; the identical ROI with that vertex removed returns 22.2405 - a 20.0% attenuation from one bad vertex out of five, exactly the (V-1)/V dilution. Second case: a 4-vertex ROI where vertex 0 is constant 5.0 in A and constant 0.0 in B (se=0, perfect separation) returns 13.0917; dropping that vertex returns 17.4556 - the most significant vertex in the ROI drags the mean DOWN because it is scored as zero. The docstring at line 322 admits only the second case ('Vertices with zero pooled variance contribute 0 rather than inf') and does not mention non-finite input at all.
findings.concrete_failure: A real 58-vertex FFCr ROI in which 12 vertices fall on the medial wall or are otherwise emitted as NaN by the model returns an ROI statistic attenuated by 12/58 = 21% relative to the truth, with nothing in the output or logs indicating that a fifth of the ROI was discarded. A borderline result at the D-3 detection floor flips from detected to NO-GO purely from unreported data loss. (Caveat: I could not verify how often TRIBE predictions actually contain non-finite vertices - see search_failures - so the code path is proven but its real-world frequency is not.)
findings.fix: Split the two cases. Raise (or return NaN) on non-finite input: `if not np.isfinite(av).all() or not np.isfinite(bv).all(): raise ValueError(...)`. For the genuine se == 0 case, keep contributing 0 only when diff is also 0, and raise or warn with a vertex count when diff != 0. Return the count of excluded vertices alongside the statistic, or at minimum log it, so silent attenuation is impossible.

findings.title: detection_floor reports a solvable configuration error as a scientific conclusion when alpha < 1/(n_perm+1)
findings.claim: achieved_power calls mc_perm_p, whose smallest possible return value is 1/(n_perm+1). If alpha is below that, no effect size of any magnitude can ever clear the threshold, so the doubling loop runs all the way to max_effect and raises a RuntimeError whose text asserts that the DESIGN is underpowered and instructs the researcher to report that. The design may in fact be perfectly well powered; the only thing wrong is n_perm. There is no validation of alpha against 1/(n_perm+1) anywhere in the function.
findings.evidence: Line 441 `mc_perm_p(a, b, n_perm=n_perm, seed=...)` returns `(ge + 1) / (n_perm + 1)` (line 160), minimum 1/(n_perm+1). Lines 447-454 raise RuntimeError with the message 'the design is underpowered for any plausible effect; report that, do not run it'. Demonstrated: `detection_floor(30, noise_sd=1.0, alpha=0.004, n_sim=5, n_perm=200)` raises after 0.3 s with 'no effect below 1000000.0 reaches 80% power at n=30, sd=1.0, alpha=0.004 - the design is underpowered for any plausible effect; report that, do not run it'. The true analytic MDE for n=30 per group at alpha=0.004 is about 0.79 sd - the design is fine. The trigger is simply 1/(200+1) = 0.004975 > 0.004. With the default n_perm=400 the boundary is 0.0024938, so Bonferroni over 11 or more tests at 0.025 crosses it.
findings.concrete_failure: The operator computes floors for 5 ROIs x 2 IUT contrasts = 10 tests and Bonferroni-corrects to alpha = 0.0025 with n_perm=400 (boundary 0.0024938 - it passes by 6e-7). Adding a sixth ROI takes alpha to 0.00208, below the boundary, and detection_floor raises. The message says the design cannot detect any plausible effect, so - following its own instruction 'report that' - the paper states the design is hopeless when the real fix is n_perm=1000. This is the project's own D-3 doctrine ('no verdict without a floor') producing a false verdict.
findings.fix: Validate up front: `if alpha <= 1.0 / (n_perm + 1): raise ValueError(f"alpha={alpha} is at or below the smallest p-value mc_perm_p can return, 1/(n_perm+1)={1/(n_perm+1):.6f}; increase n_perm to at least {int(np.ceil(1/alpha))}")`. Fail immediately with the actionable message instead of after ~21 doublings with a misleading one.

findings.title: event_locked_contrast silently drops empty other-category arrays, changing the baseline denominator without notice
findings.claim: The comprehension `others = [o for o in others if o.size]` removes any category whose response array arrived empty. Because the baseline is the mean over categories, dropping one silently changes the estimand from 'mean of K category means' to 'mean of K-1 category means'. The function raises only if ALL categories are empty. An upstream failure that loses one category therefore produces a plausible-looking number rather than an error.
findings.evidence: Line 300: `others = [o for o in others if o.size]`, then line 303 `return float(tgt.mean() - np.mean([o.mean() for o in others]))`. Run: event_locked_contrast([10., 10.], [[0., 0.], [4., 4.]]) = 8.0 (baseline = mean(0, 4) = 2). event_locked_contrast([10., 10.], [[], [4., 4.]]) = 6.0 (baseline = 4) - a 25% change in the contrast, returned with no warning. The docstring states the estimand as 'mean(target) - mean over categories of mean(category)' and says nothing about dropping categories.
findings.concrete_failure: S2's protocol is faces minus the mean of bodies/places/objects/characters. If the character category's onsets are lost upstream (a manifest typo, a dropped-segment IndexError swallowed by a caller, a category with all onsets outside the window), event_locked_contrast returns the faces-minus-three-categories contrast. Since characters/VWFA is the lowest-responding category in FFC, dropping it raises the baseline and shrinks the face contrast, biasing toward NO-GO. Nothing in the output distinguishes this from a genuine result.
findings.fix: Raise instead of filtering: `if any(o.size == 0 for o in others): raise ValueError(f"{sum(o.size == 0 for o in others)} of {len(others)} other-category arrays are empty - the baseline is the mean over CATEGORIES, so a missing category silently changes the estimand")`. If a caller genuinely needs the permissive behaviour, make it an explicit opt-in argument and return the surviving category count.

findings.title: event_locked_response double-applies the 5 s hemodynamic lag that TRIBE already bakes into its output; the S2 read lands ~5 s past the model's own peak
findings.claim: `lag_trs: int = 5` reads row `onset+5` of `preds`. But TRIBE v2's output row t is ALREADY the hemodynamically-lagged response to the stimulus at t — the 5 s HRF offset is applied at training time by the fMRI target extractor. Reading at +5 therefore reads the predicted BOLD at onset+10 s, not onset+5 s. The docstring's stated justification ('a lag of 5 TRs is 5 s — the canonical HRF peak') is exactly the double-count that two other artifacts in this same repo already warn against.
findings.evidence:
roi_stats.py:239 `lag_trs: int = 5`; :245-247 "TR is 1.0 s (source-of-truth, verified), so a lag of 5 TRs is 5 s — the canonical HRF peak"; :253 "Default 5 per the published protocol."

FOUR independent confirmations that the offset is already applied:
(1) tribev2-source/README.md:32 — "They are offset by 5 seconds in the past, in order to compensate for the hemodynamic lag."
(2) tribev2/grids/defaults.py:67 — `neuro_extractor = {"name": "FmriExtractor", ..., "offset": 5, "frequency": 1, ...}`.
(3) neuralset source (facebookresearch/neuroai, neuralset/extractors/neuro.py) — FmriExtractor docstring: `offset : float — Seconds to shift TRs forward to align delayed BOLD response.`; `_get_timed_arrays`: `out = ta.copy(start=event.start - self.offset)` then `out.overlap(start, duration)`. The BOLD series is relabelled 5 s earlier before the window is cut, so target[row i] = BOLD(window_start + i + 5). The model learns stimulus(t) -> BOLD(t+5).
(4) Meta's own tribe_demo.ipynb: cell 10 calls `plot_timesteps(preds[:15], segments=segments[:15], show_stimuli=True)`; plotting/base.py:392-395 pairs `preds[i]` with `get_clip(segment).get_frame(0)` = the frame at second i, no shift. Markdown cell 9: "as the image appears on the screen, the visual cortex lights up (t=4s), followed by the language network when the character starts to speak (t=12s)." The events dataframe printed in cell 6 shows the FIRST Word event at start=12.213 s. A +5 s lag would put the language response at panel 17, outside the 15-panel figure. Zero lag.

The repo already knows this: scripts/algonauts/prepare_submission.py:32-34 — "A3. HRF. TRIBE's own README states its predictions are already offset by 5 s ... We therefore apply NO further shift." MASTER-PLAN.md §3.8 — "note TRIBE already applies a 5 s HRF offset — do not double-apply."

Independent mechanism, from neuralset/extractors/video.py:164-165,183 (`T = clip_duration` = 4 s; `subtimes = [k/num_frames*T for k in reversed(range(num_frames))]`; `_VideoImage(video=video, time=max(0, t - t2))`): V-JEPA2's window is the TRAILING 4 s ending at each 2 Hz bin. Output row r pools bins r+0.5 and r+1.0, so row r sees video over (r-3.4375, r+1.0]. A 1 s image at [o, o+1) is inside the video encoder's receptive field for rows o..o+4 and OUTSIDE it at row o+5. (This formula reproduces D024(b)'s independently verified figures exactly: 20 bins x 64 frames = 1280, and 55+47+39+31+23+15+7 = 217 clamped frames = 17.0%.)
findings.concrete_failure: Simulated the exact S2 design (150 trials, 9 s SOA, faces 1.00 vs objects 0.60 vs places 0.55 in the ROI) with preds[r] = predicted BOLD(r+5) per the verified convention, canonical SPM double-gamma HRF. event_locked_contrast(faces, [objects, places]) returns +0.4266 at lag_trs=0 (the true effect is 0.425) and +0.0769 at lag_trs=5 — a 5.5x attenuation, matching h(10 s)/h(5 s) = 0.183. S2's GO/NO-GO and its detection floor both scale with this number, so a real, recoverable FFA/PPA/EBA effect is reported at ~18% of its size and can fail the floor. Because S2 is the pre-committed replication gate (MASTER-PLAN §6: 'S2 does not replicate -> the bug is ours. No further GPU spend until it does'), this defect converts a successful replication into a stop-the-project verdict.
findings.fix: Do not hardcode a lag. Change `event_locked_response` to return the peri-event time course (rows onset-2 .. onset+9, one array per trial) and add a thin wrapper that reduces it at a chosen lag; make S2 report the group-average evoked response and take the peak lag as MEASURED, not assumed. This costs zero GPU (it is a re-read of the same prediction array) and it is also the honest thing to publish in a paper about measurement failure modes. If a single default is kept, it must be 0, with the docstring citing README.md:32 and neuralset's FmriExtractor offset semantics, and the existing +5 retained only as the labelled comparison. Note the one piece of countervailing evidence: arXiv 2605.04326 Fig 4A says predicted activity 'peaks 5 seconds after the stimulus onset' — consistent with the same array plotted on the BOLD clock rather than the row index, but it is not proof. Sweeping the lag makes the question moot and answers it with data.

findings.title: event_locked_response indexes rows of preds but documents them as TR indices; TRIBE drops rows and concatenates windows, so the mapping silently breaks
findings.claim: `rows = np.asarray(list(onsets_tr), dtype=int) + int(lag_trs)` treats `preds` row index as absolute TR index. That identity holds only for a single timeline whose events start at t=0 and are contiguous. TRIBE's `predict()` returns ONLY kept rows and concatenates them across 100 s windows and across timelines, so the moment S2 runs more than one clip in one events frame — or any TR is dropped — row index diverges from TR index. The function has no `segments` argument and cannot detect this. Its only guard fires when the read runs off the END of the array; misalignment inside the array is silent.
findings.evidence:
roi_stats.py:268-275 — the read is `p[rows]` with `rows = onsets + lag`, guarded only by `if rows.min() < 0 or rows.max() >= p.shape[0]`. Docstring :251 calls them 'event onset rows (integer TR indices)', conflating the two.

tribev2/demo_utils.py:148 `remove_empty_segments: bool = True`; :365-380 —
```
for segment in batch.segments:
    for t in np.arange(0, segment.duration - 1e-2, self.data.TR):
        batch_segments.append(segment.copy(offset=t, duration=self.data.TR))
keep = np.array([len(s.ns_events) > 0 for s in batch_segments])
...
y_pred = rearrange(y_pred, "b d t -> (b t) d")[keep]
```
Empirically anchored in Meta's own demo notebook (cell 8 output): a 52.21 s clip prints `INFO - Predicted 53 / 100 segments (53.0% kept)` and `Predictions shape: (53, 20484)`. 47 of the window's 100 rows are dropped. `predict()` returns `all_segments` precisely so callers can recover the mapping; `event_locked_response` ignores it.
findings.concrete_failure: S2 runs 150 exemplar clips of nominally 9 s in one events frame (one timeline each — the only affordable batching, per MASTER-PLAN §3.6 where each separate `predict()` call costs ~175 s of encoder load). ffmpeg encodes some clips at 9.04 s rather than 9.00 s — the project measured exactly this spread on its own v3b clips ('All 30 clips 10.000-10.040 s', D023(g)/D024(a)) — so those clips contribute 10 kept rows instead of 9. Passing the natural onsets `i*9`: with 20% of clips one row long, the cumulative row error reaches 31 rows, 99% of trials are read from the wrong row, and event_locked_contrast returns +0.0590 instead of +0.4266. No exception is raised (array is 1373 rows, max read index 1341). The run looks clean, the numbers are noise, and the verdict is NO-GO.
findings.fix: Add a required `segments` (or `onsets_s` + `segments`) argument and resolve rows by (timeline, absolute time) from the `all_segments` list `predict()` already returns: build `{(seg.timeline, round(seg.start,3)): row}` and look each onset up, raising if any onset is absent. Additionally assert `preds.shape[0] == len(all_segments)` and, for the concatenated design, `preds.shape[0] == expected_seconds`. Never index predictions by an arithmetic formula.

findings.title: S2 must use ONE continuous concatenated video with the ISI rendered as real frames; N separate 9 s clips puts the read in a 91%-zero window, and an unrendered ISI puts it in literal zero padding that is still returned as a kept row
findings.claim: Direct answer to the lane question. With the ISI rendered as video, the onset+5 read lands in REAL model output, not padding — but only because the per-timeline dummy CategoricalEvent keeps every TR in the timeline span regardless of whether features exist there. That same mechanism is the trap: if the 8 s ISI is NOT rendered as frames (i.e. events are 1 s Video events with gaps), the ISI TRs are STILL KEPT while their video features are exact zeros, so `event_locked_response` returns numbers read from pure padding and `event_locked_contrast` measures nothing — silently. Separately, N separate 9 s clips (one timeline each) leaves each 100 s model window 91% exact zeros and puts the correct-lag read at row 0, the single most frame-0-contaminated row.
findings.evidence:
n_kept is set by the timeline span, not by feature coverage. tribev2/main.py:186-195 builds ONE dummy event per timeline spanning `start=timeline.start.min()`, `duration=timeline.stop.max() - timeline.start.min()`; demo_utils.py:371 keeps a TR iff `len(s.ns_events) > 0`; `ns_events` is overlap-based with no type filter (D023, verified against neuralset segments.py:250-262 -> 155-164 -> 89-104, `mask = (starts < stop) & (stops > start)`). So every TR inside the timeline span survives.

Empirical anchor, Meta's demo notebook cell 8: a 52.21 s Sintel clip -> `Predicted 53 / 100 segments (53.0% kept)`, shape (53, 20484). One 100 s window (duration_trs=100, defaults.py:127; TR = 1/neuro.frequency = 1.0, main.py:146-147 + defaults.py:68), 53 = ceil(52.21) contiguous rows from t=0. A 9 s clip gives 9-10 rows of 100 -> 91% zeros; a 1350 s concatenated file gives 14 windows all fully populated and preds row index == absolute second.

Zero-fill for uncovered times is the established mechanism (D023(b), neuralset extractors/base.py:250-262, 302-305 — deleted Word rows cause 'exact zeros' at the affected TRs).

Row 0 is the worst row to read: neuralset extractors/video.py `time=max(0, t - t2)` clamps every pre-clip frame to the clip's first frame; reproducing the formula gives 217/1280 = 17.0% of a 10 s clip's frames clamped to frame 0, matching D024(b) exactly.

MASTER-PLAN S2 does not state which construction it intends. Its cost line does: '5 categories x 50 x 9 s ~ 2250 s of video ~ 7.2 h' is exactly 2250 x 11.5 s/s, i.e. it uses only §3.6's per-second video term and omits the per-clip 65 s ASR and per-call 175 s load — an estimate that is only valid for a single concatenated file.
findings.concrete_failure:
Construction A (gappy events, ISI not rendered): 150 Video events of 1 s at t=0,9,18,... plus the timeline-spanning dummy. preds has ~1350 rows, all kept. Reading onset+5 (or onset+0) for any trial whose read row is not inside a 1 s image event returns the model's response to an all-zero video feature vector. Every category returns the same baseline; event_locked_contrast ~ 0 for faces, places, bodies and characters alike. S2 reports 'not recovered', MASTER-PLAN §6 fires ('Stop. Do not run S3'), and ~1.5 GPU-hours plus the paper's central replication are lost to a stimulus-encoding choice, with no error message anywhere.
Construction B (N separate 9 s clips): the read exists but sits in a window that is 91% zeros — the exact mis-specification D026 ground 4 already names ('10 s clips fill ~11 of 100 window rows') — and at the correct lag lands on row 0, where 17% of V-JEPA2's frames are the clamped first frame. Cost also blows up: 250 clips x 65 s of whisperx = 4.5 h of ASR alone on top of the planned 7.2 h.
findings.fix: Build the localizer as ONE continuous silent video file with the ISI rendered as real frames (mid-grey), preceded by a >=5 s blank lead-in to absorb the file-start frame-0 clamp. Construct the events DataFrame BY HAND — a single `{'type':'Video','filepath':...,'start':0,'timeline':'loc','subject':'default'}` row through `standardize_events` — rather than `get_events_dataframe`, so there is no Audio event, no whisper pass over silence, and no ChunkEvents (see the ChunkEvents finding). main.py:200-212 then drops the audio and text extractors (the demo notebook shows this working in reverse: 'Removing extractor video as there are no corresponding events'), and model.py:189-192 substitutes zeros. Use an SOA that divides 100 s (1 s on / 9 s ISI) so every peri-event window lies inside one model window and every trial occupies the same set of within-window positions. Randomize category order across the WHOLE sequence and never block by category: the encoder is maskless/bidirectional (config.yaml `causal: false`; neuraltrain/models/transformer.py:69-72; tribev2/model.py:233 — see data/algonauts/position_embed_dead.md), so every output row is a function of all ~10 trials in its 100 s window, and blocking would confound window identity with category. Finally assert `preds.shape[0] == round(video_duration_s)` before analysing anything.

findings.title: ChunkEvents silently deletes any chunk shorter than min_duration=30 s, and puts a frame-0 clamp at every 60 s boundary of a concatenated stimulus
findings.claim: If S2 builds its localizer through `get_events_dataframe`, the Video and Audio events are passed through `ChunkEvents(max_duration=60, min_duration=30)` with the default `tiling="max"`. Two consequences for a long concatenated stimulus: (a) the trailing piece is DROPPED, not merged, whenever its duration is below min_duration — so a localizer whose length mod 60 falls in (0, 30) silently loses its last up-to-30 s of stimulus and the trials in it; (b) the video is split into ~23 independent events, and V-JEPA2 clamps its 4 s trailing window to the FIRST FRAME OF EACH EVENT, so the first ~4 s of every 60 s chunk is visually corrupted.
findings.evidence:
tribev2/demo_utils.py:76-78 —
```
ExtractAudioFromVideo(),
ChunkEvents(event_type_to_chunk="Audio", max_duration=60, min_duration=30),
ChunkEvents(event_type_to_chunk="Video", max_duration=60, min_duration=30),
```
neuralset (facebookresearch/neuroai, neuralset/events/transforms/chunking.py), `ChunkEvents._chunk_timeline`:
```
added.extend(
    p.to_dict()
    for p in pieces
    if p.duration >= self.min_duration - self._SAMPLE_GRID_TOL
)
```
and the class docstring: `"max"`: emit chunks of exactly `max_duration` until the section is exhausted; the trailing partial chunk is dropped iff its duration is `< min_duration`' / 'Invariants ... `"max"` may silently drop sections/trailing pieces shorter than `min_duration`.'

Frame-0 clamp per event: neuralset/extractors/video.py `_get_data` does `video = event.read()` then `_VideoImage(video=video, time=max(0, t - t2))` with `subtimes` spanning a trailing `clip_duration` = 4 s. Features are computed per EVENT and only afterwards cropped (`tarray.copy(start=event.start).overlap(start, duration)`), so the clamp is to the chunk's own first frame. The formula reproduces D024(b)'s verified 1280-frame / 217-clamped figures exactly.

VERSION CAVEAT, stated rather than hidden: tribev2 pins `neuralset==0.0.2`, where this class lives in `events/transforms/etypes.py` and behaves differently in at least one respect — on the main-branch code above a 10 s Video event would be dropped entirely (10 < 30), which cannot be what 0.0.2 does because Gate 0 ran 10 s clips successfully, and source-of-truth records `etypes.py:453` discarding `t=0.0` on a strict inequality before min_duration is consulted. The trailing-drop behaviour in 0.0.2 is therefore UNVERIFIED.
findings.concrete_failure: 3 categories x 50 exemplars at a 9 s SOA = 1350 s; 1350 mod 60 = 30, exactly on the boundary — one second shorter (1349 s, or a 5 s lead-in making 1355 s trimmed anywhere) and the last 29 s of Video and Audio events vanish. The timeline span shrinks with them, so preds is ~1320 rows instead of ~1350 and the last 3 trials never existed. At lag 0 or 5 that raises IndexError (loud, recoverable); but if the trailing loss is smaller than the read lag, or if trials are dropped from the middle of a category, the contrast is silently computed on an unbalanced set. Separately, with 23 chunks, ~4 s after each boundary is frame-0-clamped — at a 9 s SOA that is ~6.7% of trials with corrupted visual features, and with a 10 s SOA it is deterministically the first trial of every chunk (25 of 150).
findings.fix: Bypass ChunkEvents entirely by hand-building the events DataFrame with a single unchunked Video event and no Audio event (see the S2 construction finding) — this removes both problems at once, at the cost of one large exca cache entry instead of 23. If `get_events_dataframe` is used, make the total stimulus duration an exact multiple of 60 s, assert `preds.shape[0] == round(duration_s)` immediately after `predict()`, and pre-register exclusion of any trial whose onset falls in the first 4 s of a 60 s chunk. Before either, spend 2 CPU-minutes resolving the version caveat: `python -c "import neuralset.events.transforms.etypes as m; print(m.__file__)"` on the pinned 0.0.2 wheel and read the ChunkEvents body.

findings.title: At lag_trs=5 roughly 6% of trials are read from a 100 s window whose input never contained the stimulus; at lag 0 the figure is exactly zero
findings.claim: The 100 s windows are non-overlapping and each is a separate forward pass, so a read row in window k+1 is computed from features that contain nothing from window k. With a 9 s SOA, every onset with `onset mod 100 >= 95` has its onset+5 read in the next window — a row the flashed image could not have influenced. Those trials contribute pure baseline to their category mean. The defect exists only because of the +5; with the correct lag the read row is always in the same window as the image.
findings.evidence: tribev2/grids/defaults.py:127-129 — `"duration_trs": 100, "overlap_trs_train": 0, "overlap_trs_val": 0`. tribev2/main.py:245-251 — `ns.segments.list_segments(..., stride=(self.duration_trs - overlap_trs) * self.TR, duration=self.duration_trs * self.TR, ...)`, so stride == duration == 100 s: contiguous, non-overlapping tiling. Each window is one batch element through `model(batch)` (demo_utils.py:377), with no cross-window state.
findings.concrete_failure: 3 categories x 50 exemplars at 9 s SOA (1350 s, 14 windows): 9 of 150 trials (6.0%) have onset//100 != (onset+5)//100. 5 categories x 50 at 9 s SOA (2250 s): 14 of 250 (5.6%). Each such trial contributes a baseline row to its category mean, diluting the contrast by ~6% on top of the 5.5x lag attenuation. Because the affected onsets are a fixed arithmetic subset (onset mod 100 in 95..99) and category order is randomized, the dilution is unbiased but unmodelled and unreported. At lag 0, zero trials are affected.
findings.fix: Fix the lag (see the first finding), which removes this entirely. Additionally choose an SOA that divides 100 s — 1 s on / 9 s ISI gives exactly 10 trials per model window, so the whole peri-event time course (rows onset-2 .. onset+9) stays inside one window for every trial except the first and last two of each window; record the deviation from Meta's 8 s SOA. Whatever SOA is chosen, compute and report `sum((onset//100) != ((onset+lag)//100))` in the run manifest so the count is never implicit.

findings.title: MASTER-PLAN S2's 'audio and text extractors are dropped when no matching events exist' is false for a silent video built through get_events_dataframe
findings.claim: The extractor-dropping mechanism is real, but `get_audio_and_text_events` runs `ExtractAudioFromVideo()` unconditionally before it. A silent-but-present audio track therefore produces an Audio event, the audio extractor is NOT dropped, whisperx runs over silence (a documented hallucination risk this repo already mitigates elsewhere), and any hallucinated Word events pull in the text extractor too.
findings.evidence:
tribev2/demo_utils.py:75-79 —
```
transforms = [
    ExtractAudioFromVideo(),
    ChunkEvents(event_type_to_chunk="Audio", max_duration=60, min_duration=30),
    ChunkEvents(event_type_to_chunk="Video", max_duration=60, min_duration=30),
]
```
with `ExtractWordsFromAudio()` appended unless `audio_only`. The dropping rule that the plan relies on is main.py:200-212 and only fires when no event of the extractor's type exists at all — it runs AFTER these transforms. The repo already treats whisper-over-silence as a live hazard: scripts/algonauts/predict_ood.py docstring and `--mask-text-for chaplin` ('the choice is between feeding TRIBE whatever Whisper hallucinates over a music-only track, or giving it no text events at all').
findings.concrete_failure: S2 renders its localizer with ffmpeg, which emits a silent AAC track by default when muxing to mp4. `get_events_dataframe(video_path=...)` creates an Audio event spanning the file, whisperx transcribes ~1350 s of silence, and any hallucinated words are fed to LLaMA-3.2. The run costs an extra ~23 whisperx invocations and an audio-encoder pass that the 7.2 h budget does not include, and injects an uncontrolled text signal into a contrast that is supposed to be purely visual — so an in-silico VWFA/character result could be driven by hallucinated text rather than by the flashed characters.
findings.fix: Build the events DataFrame by hand with only a Video row (no Audio, no Words), which makes the drop rule fire for real; or render the video with `-an` and verify no Audio event is produced. Either way, log the event-type counts and the ASR word count before `predict()`, as predict_ood.py already does. Also correct the S2 cost line: 2250 s x 11.5 s/s = 7.2 h counts only the video term of §3.6 and is valid solely for a single concatenated file; 250 separate 9 s clips would add ~4.5 h of ASR (250 x 65 s) plus ~12 h of per-call encoder loads if run one predict() per clip.

lanes.lane_summary:
DEFINITIVE ANSWER TO THE LANE QUESTION. An event-locked read at onset+5 s does NOT land in zero padding — but it lands 5 s past the model's own response peak, and the reason it never looks like padding is itself the trap. I traced the whole chain against primary artifacts: n_kept is set by the per-timeline dummy CategoricalEvent (main.py:186-195) and the keep rule `len(s.ns_events) > 0` (demo_utils.py:371), so EVERY TR inside the timeline span is returned regardless of whether any extractor produced features there. Meta's own demo notebook gives the empirical anchor: a 52.21 s clip prints "Predicted 53 / 100 segments (53.0% kept)" — one 100 s window, 53 contiguous rows from t=0, 47 rows of padding dropped. So: with the 8 s ISI rendered as real video frames, the read is inside real output; with a gappy event list (1 s image events, no ISI frames) the ISI rows are still KEPT while their video features are exact zeros, and event_locked_contrast would return ~0 for every category with no error raised. That is the paper-sinking silent failure, and S2 has not specified which construction it uses.

The bigger finding is the lag itself. TRIBE v2's predictions are already shifted 5 s to compensate for the hemodynamic delay — confirmed four ways: README.md:32 verbatim; defaults.py:67 `FmriExtractor(offset=5)`; neuralset's FmriExtractor source ("Seconds to shift TRs forward to align delayed BOLD response", `ta.copy(start=event.start - self.offset)`); and Meta's demo notebook, which pairs prediction row t with the stimulus frame at second t and reports the language network at panel t=12 when the first Word event is at 12.213 s. `event_locked_response(lag_trs=5)` therefore reads predicted BOLD(onset+10). Canonical HRF: 18.3% of peak, a 5.5x attenuation, reproduced numerically (+0.077 recovered of a true +0.427). Independently, neuralset's video extractor uses a TRAILING 4 s V-JEPA2 window (its formula reproduces D024(b)'s verified 1280-frame/217-clamped numbers exactly), so at lag 5 the flashed image has left the visual encoder's receptive field entirely. This repo already recorded the correct fact twice (prepare_submission.py A3; MASTER-PLAN §3.8 "do not double-apply") and the new code does it anyway.

RECOMMENDATION for S2's stimulus. (1) One continuous silent video file, ISI rendered as real mid-grey frames, >=5 s blank lead-in; total duration an exact multiple of 60 s. (2) Build the events DataFrame by hand — a single Video row, no Audio event — so the audio/text extractors are genuinely dropped (main.py:200-212), whisper never runs over silence, and ChunkEvents never splits the file (which would drop the trailing chunk if <30 s and frame-0-clamp the first 4 s of all ~23 chunks). (3) SOA that divides 100 s (1 s on / 9 s ISI, 10 trials per model window) so no peri-event window crosses a 100 s boundary; record the deviation from Meta's 8 s. (4) Randomize category order across the whole sequence, never block — the encoder is maskless/bidirectional over the full 100 s window, so blocking confounds window identity with category. (5) Never index preds arithmetically: resolve rows from `all_segments` by (timeline, time) and assert `preds.shape[0] == round(duration_s)`. (6) Do not hardcode lag 5 — extract the peri-event time course and report the MEASURED peak lag; it costs zero GPU and it settles the one remaining ambiguity by measurement.

Residual uncertainty, and what would close it: arXiv 2605.04326 Fig 4A says predicted activity "peaks 5 seconds after the stimulus onset", which is consistent with the same array plotted on the BOLD clock rather than the row index, but I could not retrieve Methods §5.9 to confirm (see search_failures). Cost to close: read §5.9 of the PDF by hand (~10 minutes, free), or simply sweep the lag in S2, which answers it empirically at zero cost. Second residual: ChunkEvents' trailing-drop and short-event behaviour is verified on neuralset main, and tribev2 pins neuralset==0.0.2 where the class lives in events/transforms/etypes.py and demonstrably differs in at least one respect. Cost to close: `python -c "import neuralset.events.transforms.etypes as m; print(m.__file__)"` on the pinned wheel and read the ChunkEvents body — ~2 CPU-minutes, no GPU. Both are cheap and both should be done before the S2 stimulus is frozen.

lanes.lane_summary:
I checked `event_locked_response` / `event_locked_contrast` (and the `glm_contrast_z` fidelity claim attached to them) against the actual published protocol, which I retrieved rather than assumed: I downloaded https://arxiv.org/html/2605.04326v1 with curl into the scratchpad and read §2.5, §5.9 and the Fig-4 caption verbatim. Authoritative text, §5.9 "Contrast maps": *"To obtain contrast maps for the visual experiments, we obtain contrast maps by simply selecting the predicted response at t=5 after the image is shown (which is the peak of the response as shown in fig. 4A), and substracting the average responses at t=5 for the other categories."* Timing, §5.9 and §2.5 (twice): *"flashed for 1 second every 8 seconds"*. GLM, §5.9: used only for the **language** experiments, via *"a General Linear Model (GLM), where the regressors are estimated through the convolution of TRIBE's predicted BOLD responses with the canonical Hemodynamic Response Function... nilearn's FirstLevelModel with default parameters"*. ROI mapping, §5.9: *"FFA, EBA, PPA, VWFA, A5, 45, STS, TPJ, MTG respectively correspond to the following ROI labels: FFC, V4t, PH, A5, 45, STSv, PGi, TE1a"*.

VERDICT ON THE CORE QUESTION: the single-TR read at onset+5 is CORRECT and faithful — the paper says "simply selecting the predicted response at t=5", not a window average, and `event_locked_response` does exactly that. Excluding the target category from the baseline is also correct. The per-vertex-then-average order in `glm_contrast_z` matches Fig 4E ("z-scores are averaged for all cortical vertices falling within the parcel"). I could find no defect in the lag-5 read itself.

What I did find sits around the statistic rather than inside it: (1) `glm_contrast_z`'s docstring claims to be "what Meta's Fig 4 actually reports", which §5.9 contradicts — the visual contrasts use no GLM at all, and the paper's GLM is a nilearn FirstLevelModel on the time-series with HRF-convolved regressors and AR(1) noise, not a two-sample pooled-SE z over clip rows; (2) `event_locked_response` indexes prediction rows as if they were TR indices, but the only producer in this pipeline (`TribeModel.predict`) returns `(n_kept_segments, n_vertices)` with empty segments dropped and no row→time map — the project's own interface contract flags exactly this, and Gate 0's own 10.000-vs-10.040 s clips demonstrably yield 10 vs 11 rows; (3) the ROI labels the S2 replication plans to report are not Meta's, and our EBA proxy physically contains Meta's PPA parcel; (4) S2's stimulus timing (1 s + 8 s ISI = 9 s SOA) is not the paper's 8 s SOA; (5) `onsets_tr`/`lag_trs` silently truncate floats and there is no TR parameter, so the TR=1.0 s coincidence is load-bearing and unguarded; (6) the API cannot produce the whole-brain contrast *map* that is the paper's actual validated object. I ran the test suite (26 passed, 3.96 s) and verified the truncation and empty-category behaviours by direct execution. I did NOT find any place where the code assumes a TR other than 1.0 s. Separately, and outside my lane so only noted here: `ops/interface-contracts.md` has no entry for `tribe_tools/roi_stats.py` at all, though CLAUDE.md rule 2 makes updating it mandatory before adding these seven public functions.

findings.title: glm_contrast_z is attributed to the paper's Fig 4, but §5.9 says the visual contrasts use no GLM and the paper's GLM is a different estimator entirely
findings.claim: The docstring asserts "What Meta's Fig 4 actually reports, and non-compositional". The paper's own methods section says the visual contrast maps in Fig 4 are computed with no GLM at all (just the t=5 subtraction), and that where a GLM is used — the language experiments — it is nilearn's FirstLevelModel with HRF-convolved regressors fit on the predicted time-series, which is not a two-sample pooled-SE z over clip rows. The fidelity claim is false as written, and the paper is internally inconsistent between its Fig-4 caption and §5.9, which the code presents as settled.
findings.evidence: arXiv 2605.04326 §5.9, verbatim: "To obtain contrast maps for the visual experiments, we obtain contrast maps by simply selecting the predicted response at t=5 after the image is shown (which is the peak of the response as shown in fig. 4 A), and substracting the average responses at t=5 for the other categories." and, separately, "To obtain contrast maps for the lanugage experiments, we follow the protocol used for the IBC dataset. Specifically, we fit a General Linear Model (GLM), where the regressors are estimated through the convolution of TRIBE's predicted BOLD responses with the canonical Hemodynamic Response Function. We use the implementation provided by nilearn's FirstLevelModel with default parameters." The Fig 4 caption says the opposite of §5.9 for the visual case: "Experimental images are flashed for 1 second, with an interval of 8 seconds, and a general linear model (GLM) is fit on the predicted time-series to obtain z-scored contrast maps (see section 5.9 for details)." The code, meanwhile, is `var = ((na - 1) * av.var(axis=0, ddof=1) + (nb - 1) * bv.var(axis=0, ddof=1)) / (na + nb - 2)` / `se = np.sqrt(var * (1.0 / na + 1.0 / nb))` — a two-sample pooled-variance z over observation rows, with no design matrix, no HRF convolution, and no AR(1) whitening (nilearn FirstLevelModel defaults to noise_model='ar1', hrf_model='glover', high_pass=0.01).
findings.concrete_failure: The ICBINB-BIO paper says, on the strength of this docstring and D027, that it reproduces the model authors' own Fig-4 GLM statistic. A reviewer who opens §5.9 finds (i) the visual localizer results the project cites for FFA/PPA/EBA/VWFA recovery involve no GLM, and (ii) the paper's GLM is an AR(1)-whitened nilearn time-series fit, not this estimator. The project's central methodological move — "we retracted a compositional statistic and adopted the model authors' own" — is then shown to misdescribe the authors' own. This is the same class of error (asserting a protocol detail without checking the source) that produced the 07-31 retraction, at a point where there is no time to recover.
findings.fix: Rewrite the docstring to state what is true and what is chosen: `glm_contrast_z` is a per-vertex two-sample contrast z averaged over the ROI, structurally matching Fig 4E's "z-scores are averaged for all cortical vertices falling within the parcel", but it is NOT the paper's estimator. Record verbatim in ops/source-of-truth.md that §5.9 uses the plain t=5 subtraction for the visual localizers and nilearn FirstLevelModel (HRF-convolved regressors, AR(1)) only for the language ones, and flag the caption/§5.9 inconsistency explicitly. If the paper is to claim reproduction of the authors' GLM, use nilearn FirstLevelModel; otherwise state the deviation. Also note in the docstring that the returned parcel-averaged value is not itself distributed as a z (measured null sd 0.230 at 20 independent vertices, i.e. ~1/sqrt(n_vertices)), so it must always be tested by permutation — as scripts/detection_floor_table.py correctly already does — and never against 1.96.

findings.title: event_locked_response indexes prediction rows as TR indices, but TribeModel.predict returns kept-segment rows with no row->time map
findings.claim: The function documents `preds: (n_trs, n_vertices)` and computes `rows = onsets_tr + lag_trs` as direct row indices. The only producer of `preds` in this project returns `(n_kept_segments, n_vertices)` — segments with no events are dropped — and the row->time mapping lives in the `all_segments` list that this API neither accepts nor mentions. Nothing checks the assumption, so a misaligned read is silent, which is the project's declared signature bug class.
findings.evidence: tribev2/demo_utils.py predict(): `for t in np.arange(0, segment.duration - 1e-2, self.data.TR): batch_segments.append(segment.copy(offset=t, duration=self.data.TR))`, then `keep = np.array([len(s.ns_events) > 0 for s in batch_segments])`, `y_pred = rearrange(y_pred, "b d t -> (b t) d")[keep]`, returning "preds : np.ndarray Array of shape ``(n_kept_segments, n_vertices)``" plus "all_segments : list Corresponding segment objects aligned with *preds*". ops/interface-contracts.md states it too: "IMPORTANT: n_kept_segments <= n_total_segments because empty segments are removed". The audited code ignores all of this: `rows = np.asarray(list(onsets_tr), dtype=int) + int(lag_trs)` ... `return p[rows][:, verts].mean(axis=1)`, with the only guard being a bounds check.
findings.concrete_failure: D028 mandates "one unique `timeline` per clip" for batched runs and makes the prediction bank the project spine, so a bank read is a concatenation of per-clip row blocks. Block lengths are not constant: the dummy CategoricalEvent spans `timeline.start.min()` to `timeline.stop.max()` (main.py:186-195) and overlap is `mask = (starts < stop) & (stops > start)`, so a 10.000 s clip keeps rows t=0..9 (10 rows) while a 10.040 s clip keeps t=0..10 (11 rows). Gate 0 v3b's own delivered clips are certified at "10.000-10.040 s" (D023(g)/D024(a)), i.e. both lengths are present in the existing stimulus set. A caller who computes global onsets from the stimulus manifest and calls event_locked_response on the concatenated bank therefore reads the wrong row for every clip after the first length mismatch, with no error — a t=+5 read that silently lands on t=+4 or on a neighbouring clip, producing a contrast that is neither the paper's nor anything else.
findings.fix: Either (a) make the API take the segment list: `event_locked_response(preds, segments, verts, onsets_s, lag_s, tr)` and resolve each onset+lag to a row by matching `segment.offset`/start times, raising if the required time is absent from `segments`; or (b) keep the row-index API but require an explicit `row_times` argument (seconds per row) and assert it is contiguous and uniformly spaced before indexing. Minimum acceptable version if neither is done before the deadline: rename the parameter to make the contract unmissable and assert at the call site in S2 that `len(preds) == expected_n_trs` for the single-timeline case, and forbid the function on multi-timeline concatenations.

findings.title: S2's replication ROIs are not the paper's ROI labels, and our EBA proxy contains the paper's PPA parcel
findings.symbol: S2 - The replication (ROI reporting list, line ~394)
findings.claim: S2 is specified as reproducing the published in-silico localizer result and its failure branch is "Not recovered -> we have a bug". But the ROI definitions frozen by the project are not the ones the paper used. The paper names single Glasser parcels; the project uses multi-parcel unions that cross-contaminate the very categories being dissociated.
findings.evidence: arXiv 2605.04326 §5.9, verbatim: "To extract regions of interest, we used the Glasser Multimodal parcellation (40). FFA, EBA, PPA, VWFA, A5, 45, STS, TPJ, MTG respectively correspond to the following ROI labels: FFC, V4t, PH, A5, 45, STSv, PGi, TE1a." (The list is 9 names to 8 labels — VWFA's label is missing — but the A5->A5 and 45->45 anchors fix the alignment of the first three: FFA=FFC, EBA=V4t, PPA=PH.) The project's frozen definitions, D021: "Specificity controls = V1 (low-level) + EBA proxy (right LO2 u LO3 u V4t u FST u PH ...)" and "Positive control = PPA (PHA1-3 u VMV1-3)". So our single EBA proxy contains BOTH of Meta's EBA parcel (V4t) and Meta's PPA parcel (PH), while our PPA (PHA1-3 u VMV1-3) shares no parcel with Meta's PPA at all.
findings.concrete_failure: S2 runs the flashed localizer, reports "EBA" from a 5-parcel union that includes the paper's PPA, and reports "PPA" from a 6-parcel union the paper never used. If bodies>others fails to separate from places>others, the branch rule sends the project to "Stop. Do not run S3. Debug against Meta's protocol" — burning the remaining days of a 9-day runway chasing a pipeline bug that is actually an ROI-definition mismatch. Conversely a spurious place-body crossover could be read as successful replication. Either way the headline sentence "we reproduced the published in-silico localizer" is not supported, because the parcels differ.
findings.fix: Add the §5.9 ROI table to ops/source-of-truth.md as a FROM-DOCS fact (FFA=FFC, EBA=V4t, PPA=PH, A5=A5, 45=45, STS=STSv, TPJ=PGi, MTG=TE1a; VWFA label not stated in the paper — record that gap explicitly rather than guessing left-FFC). In S2, report Meta's exact parcels as the replication-of-record, and report our Gate 0 unions only as a clearly labelled secondary, so the comparison to the published result is like-for-like and the Gate 0 numbers stay interpretable beside it.

findings.title: S2 encodes a 9 s stimulus-onset asynchrony; the paper's methods say 8 s
findings.claim: The plan reads the ambiguous Fig-4 caption ("flashed for 1 second, with an interval of 8 seconds") as 1 s on + 8 s off = 9 s per exemplar, and states this is "Meta's timing". The paper's results and methods text both say "one second every eight seconds", i.e. an 8 s SOA (1 s on, 7 s off).
findings.evidence: arXiv 2605.04326 §2.5: "various categories of images (fig. 4B) are flashed for 1 second every 8 seconds." §5.9: "All images are presented to TRIBE in a randomized order, for one second every eight seconds (transforming them to static videos)." MASTER-PLAN S2: "Flashed-image localizer as silent video: **1 s on / 8 s ISI** (Meta's timing)" and "Cost: 5 categories x 50 x 9 s ~ 2250 s of video ~ 7.2 h ... cut to 3 categories (faces, objects, places) x 50 = 1350 s ~ 4.3 h, or keep 5 categories at 25 exemplars ~ 3.6 h."
findings.concrete_failure: The replication is run at 9 s SOA and the write-up states "we follow Meta's 1 s/8 s for comparability and record the deviation" — a sentence that is itself the deviation, since the paper's SOA is 8 s. Every GPU-cost figure in S2 is inflated by 12.5% (2250 s vs 2000 s for the 5x50 design; 1350 s vs 1200 s for 3x50), which matters on borrowed compute with nine days left. And if the replication comes out weak, the 1 s timing difference in the inter-stimulus recovery window becomes an uncontrolled explanation the project cannot rule out.
findings.fix: Set the SOA to 8 s (1 s image, 7 s blank) in the S2 stimulus builder, recompute the cost table (5x50 = 2000 s; 3x50 = 1200 s; 5x25 = 1000 s), and record in ops/source-of-truth.md that the paper states the timing three times, twice unambiguously as "one second every eight seconds" and once ambiguously in the Fig-4 caption, with the methods text taken as authoritative.

findings.title: No TR parameter anywhere, and onsets_tr / lag_trs silently truncate floats
findings.claim: The published protocol is specified in seconds (t=5 s after onset, 8 s SOA) but the API is specified in TRs, with no `tr` argument to convert between them. TR=1.0 s makes the two numerically identical today, so nothing in the code or tests can catch a unit error. Worse, both the onset array and the lag are coerced with truncating integer casts, so passing seconds — or a correctly converted non-integer lag — fails silently rather than loudly.
findings.evidence: Code: `rows = np.asarray(list(onsets_tr), dtype=int) + int(lag_trs)`. Docstring: "TR is 1.0 s (source-of-truth, verified), so a lag of 5 TRs is 5 s". Executed just now: with a 40-row array where the intended peak sits at row 9, `event_locked_response(p, verts, [8.0], lag_trs=5/2.0)` returns `[0.]` — `int(2.5)` truncates to 2 — and `event_locked_response(p, verts, [8.9], lag_trs=0.9)` returns a value with no error, `8.9` having been truncated to row 8 and `0.9` to 0. Neither call raises. TR itself is a model-config property (`main.py:147: return 1 / self.neuro.frequency`, neuro `frequency: 1` in grids/defaults.py:68), not a constant of the API.
findings.concrete_failure: A future checkpoint, dataset, or the MCP read path with TR != 1.0 s — the whole point of the prediction bank is that strangers re-analyse it — passes onsets in seconds or a converted lag of 5/TR. At TR=2.0 s the intended 5 s peak read becomes a 4 s read, at TR=1.49 s (HCP) it becomes int(3.36)=3 TRs = 4.47 s, and in both cases the function returns numbers rather than an error. The contrast is then off the HRF peak by 1-2 s in an unreported direction, and the result is indistinguishable from a genuine null.
findings.fix: Add an explicit `tr: float` argument (no default, or default 1.0 with the value echoed into any recorded provenance), take `onsets_s` and `lag_s` in seconds, and convert internally with an exactness check — raise if `onset_s / tr` or `lag_s / tr` is not within a small tolerance of an integer, rather than truncating. At minimum, reject non-integral `onsets_tr` / `lag_trs` inputs with a ValueError instead of casting them.

findings.title: The published object is a whole-brain contrast map; the API can only return an ROI scalar
findings.claim: `event_locked_response` averages over vertices unconditionally, so the pair cannot produce the per-vertex contrast map that is the paper's actual deliverable and the basis of its validation against IBC.
findings.evidence: Code: `return p[rows][:, verts].mean(axis=1)` — the vertex axis is collapsed before the value is ever returned, and `event_locked_contrast` then consumes 1-D per-event arrays. The paper's Fig 4 reports "C. Contrast maps obtained from TRIBE's predictions" and "E. Numerical agreement between ground truth and predicted z-scores. Each dot represents one of the 360 parcels from the HCP parcellation (40), and z-scores are averaged for all cortical vertices falling within the parcel." MASTER-PLAN S4 names exactly this as the cheap validation route: "spatial correlation of our in-silico contrast map against **IBC's** real contrast map on NeuroVault — Meta's own validation move, no fMRI download."
findings.concrete_failure: S4's NeuroVault/IBC spatial-correlation check — the cheapest external validation available and the one the model authors themselves used — cannot be run through this API. Producing the 20,484-vertex map requires either 20,484 separate calls with `verts=[v]`, or reimplementing the read outside the audited, tested module, which is where the 07-31 analysis bugs lived.
findings.fix: Give `event_locked_response` a `reduce: bool = True` flag (or add `event_locked_response_map`) returning the `(n_events, n_vertices)` slice unreduced, and let `event_locked_contrast` operate elementwise on arrays so it returns a `(n_vertices,)` contrast map when fed maps. The ROI scalar is then the ROI mean of the map, which is numerically identical to the current path for this linear contrast, so nothing already computed changes.

findings.title: The 'other categories' baseline is a mean-of-category-means the paper never specifies, and empty categories are dropped silently
findings.claim: The docstring presents mean-of-category-means as "the second half of the published protocol". The paper's phrase is ambiguous and, read literally, favours pooling exemplars; the two coincide only for a balanced design. Separately, categories that arrive empty are dropped from the baseline without any warning, silently changing what the contrast is against.
findings.evidence: arXiv 2605.04326 §5.9: "...and substracting the average responses at t=5 for the other categories" — the paper states neither pooling nor per-category averaging. Code: `others = [o for o in others if o.size]` then `return float(tgt.mean() - np.mean([o.mean() for o in others]))`, documented as "each category is averaged first, then those category means are averaged, so a category with more exemplars does not dominate the baseline". Executed just now: `event_locked_contrast([10.0, 10.0], [[], [0.0, 0.0]])` returns `10.0` — the empty category vanishes and only a ValueError for *all* categories empty remains.
findings.concrete_failure: If S2 ships unbalanced categories (the plan already contemplates trading exemplars against categories: "3 categories ... x 50" or "5 categories at 25"), or if attrition removes exemplars unevenly, the reported contrast is not the paper's and the write-up's claim to have implemented the published baseline is unsupported. The silent-drop path is worse: a category whose events all fell outside the prediction window, or that was mis-keyed by name, produces a contrast against a smaller set of categories with no log line, no warning, and no way to notice from the returned float — the exact silent-failure class the project set out to eliminate.
findings.fix: Soften the docstring to say the paper does not disambiguate, state that this implementation averages category means, and note the two are identical for a balanced design. Add an `exemplar_pooled: bool = False` switch so both readings can be reported. Replace the silent filter with a raise (or an explicit warning plus a returned count) when any supplied category is empty, so a missing category is loud.

I tried to kill this and could not. Re-derived independently: my own equicorrelated simulation (V=58, na=nb=15, 4000 reps) gives null SD 0.135 / 0.470 / 0.734 / 0.909 / 1.005 / 1.041 at rho = 0 / .2 / .5 / .8 / .95 / 1, matching the finding within MC error, with null mean 0 throughout. I then pushed past the finding's own evidence into this repo's actual design. Using scripts/compositional_demo.build_brain at D_AUD=0.24, n=15/group (the v3b design as coded in detection_floor_table.py): mean inter-vertex noise correlation in the FFCr parcel is 0.152 and the measured null SD of glm_contrast_z is 0.473. Comparing the calibrated permutation rule against a naive z>1.96 rule on the identical numbers, power is 0.52 vs 0.03 at a true effect of 0.020, 0.87 vs 0.21 at 0.030, and 1.00 vs 0.90 at 0.050 (the project's own flagship-test effect size). The naive threshold roughly doubles the detection floor, ~0.025 -> ~0.055. A genuine +0.03 FFCr effect would be reported as no selectivity by the normal threshold while the design actually had 87% power — the same shape as the 2026-07-31 retraction, at a venue whose entire topic is this class of error.

Why it clears the "changes a conclusion" bar despite no wrong number today: the docstring at roi_stats.py:461 says "What Meta's Fig 4 actually reports", the name says z, the Returns section says "Mean per-vertex z over the ROI" with no scale caveat, ops/interface-contracts.md:443 repeats the framing, and MASTER-PLAN.md:392 commits S2 to "Also compute glm_contrast_z. Report both" for FFC-right, PPA, EBA, VWFA and V1. A number named z, documented as the same quantity a published figure reports, printed beside four other ROIs, will be read on the z scale by the author and by every reviewer. Nothing in the code or tests prevents that. This is a live trap, not a theoretical one.

Two parts of the finding do not hold and I have narrowed them. (1) Its failure narrative asserts "with realistic TRIBE prediction correlation the ROI statistic's null width is well under 1". That is unsupported and arguably backwards: TRIBE predictions are spatially smooth deterministic functions of the stimulus, so across-clip residuals within a 58-vertex parcel plausibly have high rho, which pushes null SD toward 1, not away from it. The rho~0.15 I measured is an artifact of the toy brain's independent per-vertex noise term, not evidence about TRIBE. The honest claim is that the scale is undefined and unmeasured, and wrong in either direction — conservative if rho is low, anti-conservative (6% nominal 5%) if rho is near 1. (2) Its top-end figure 1.057 exceeds the theoretical ceiling sqrt(28/26) = 1.038; immaterial but it should not be pinned in a test as written.

Severity stays minor, at the top of that band. No published or computed number is currently wrong: detection_floor_table.py:75-88 is the sole consumer and it permutes the statistic against itself, which is the correct handling, and tests/test_roi_stats.py:380-395 only pin locality and an arity guard. The fix is a docstring warning plus a rename, costing minutes.
maths\\n|glm_contrast_z is documented an.correction:
Narrower, defensible version:

DEFECT (naming and documentation, not arithmetic). glm_contrast_z returns the arithmetic mean of V per-vertex two-sample t-statistics (df = na+nb-2). Its null distribution is centred at 0 but its null SD is sqrt((rho_bar + (1-rho_bar)/V) * df/(df-2)), where rho_bar is the mean inter-vertex correlation of the across-observation residuals — a nuisance parameter unrelated to the effect. Verified independently at V=58, na=nb=15: SD 0.135 (rho=0), 0.470 (0.2), 0.734 (0.5), 0.909 (0.8), 1.041 (rho=1, the theoretical ceiling sqrt(df/(df-2))=1.038). The value is therefore NOT on the z scale: it cannot be thresholded at 1.96 or 3.1, passed through a normal CDF, or compared numerically to a per-vertex z-map — which is precisely what the docstring's "What Meta's Fig 4 actually reports" invites.

CONSEQUENCE, quantified in this repo's own design (compositional_demo brain, D_AUD=0.24, n=15/group, FFCr 58 vtx): rho_bar = 0.152, null SD = 0.473. Power of the calibrated permutation test vs a z>1.96 rule: 0.52 vs 0.03 at effect 0.020; 0.87 vs 0.21 at 0.030; 1.00 vs 0.90 at 0.050. The naive threshold roughly doubles the detection floor (~0.025 -> ~0.055), so a real +0.03 effect reads as "no selectivity survives correction".

DROP from the original finding: the assertion that realistic TRIBE correlation makes the null width "well under 1". rho_bar for real TRIBE predictions is unmeasured, and high spatial smoothness argues for rho near 1 (null SD near 1, nominal 5% actually ~6%). The rho~0.15 above is a property of the synthetic brain's independent per-vertex noise, not of TRIBE. State the defect as "scale undefined and unmeasured", wrong in either direction.

FIX (cheap, do before S2):
1. Rename to roi_mean_t (or glm_contrast_meant) in roi_stats.py and ops/interface-contracts.md:443, per CLAUDE.md rule 2.
2. Replace the Returns line with a hard warning: "Mean of per-vertex t-statistics, df = na+nb-2. Its null SD is approximately sqrt(rho_bar + (1-rho_bar)/V) and is NOT 1 — measured 0.14 (rho=0) to 1.04 (rho=1) at V=58, n=15. Must be calibrated by permutation. Never threshold at a normal quantile; never compare numerically to a published per-vertex z-map."
3. Remove or qualify "What Meta's Fig 4 actually reports" — it is the sentence that makes the wrong comparison look sanctioned (and it is separately under audit for across-time vs across-observations).

maths\\n|glm_contrast_z is documented an.correction:
Two narrowings to the finding as written.

1. The proposed docstring wording "Its null SD is approximately sqrt(rho_bar)" is imprecise and understates the small-V and small-df terms. The correct expression, which I confirmed against simulation at six values of rho, is null SD ≈ sqrt((rho_bar + (1 - rho_bar)/V) * df/(df-2)) with df = na+nb-2. At rho_bar=0 this is 0.136 (not 0), and at rho_bar=1 it is 1.038 (not 1.0). Use that form in the warning and in the pinned test.

2. The failure paragraph reads as internally inconsistent — it invokes "realistic TRIBE prediction correlation" to argue the null width is "well under 1", while the brief's framing is a pathology at HIGH correlation, where the width is actually closest to 1. The defensible statement is scale-indeterminacy, not a directional bias: the null SD is governed by an unmeasured nuisance (rho_bar) and can land anywhere in 0.14-1.04, so the returned number is uninterpretable on the z scale in either direction. Concretely, on this project's own synthetic design rho_bar = 0.202 and the null SD is 0.474, so a 1.96 threshold has essentially zero size and zero power there; whether real TRIBE predictions sit at that end or near rho_bar -> 1 is unknown and unmeasured, which is precisely the defect.

Also worth noting for whoever fixes it: an ROI-averaged statistic is not numerically comparable to Meta's per-vertex Fig 4 z-map even if it were correctly scaled, since the two aggregate over different numbers of observations. So the docstring line "What Meta's Fig 4 actually reports" should be softened regardless of how the scale issue is resolved.

silent\\n|glm_contrast_z's `se > 0` mask.correction:
The finding stands, with three adjustments.

1. STRENGTHEN the zero-variance half. It is not limited to "constant only up to float32 rounding (se ~ 1e-17)". A genuinely constant vertex already breaks the documented guarantee, because np.var(ddof=1) of a constant column is nonzero (~1e-32) whenever the value's mean is not exactly representable in binary: np.full(15, 0.7).var(ddof=1) = 1.32e-32. Verified magnitude on a realistic 58-vertex ROI: clean z = 13.977 -> 2.60e14 with one constant vertex. Important carve-out: a constant-ZERO vertex is safe (var is exactly 0.0, guard fires correctly), so the medial-wall / dead-vertex case most likely to occur in fsaverage5 output is the one case that works. The exposure is a constant NONZERO vertex, e.g. a saturated or bias-only readout unit.

2. ADD the silence asymmetry, which is the strongest argument for the "silent" lane. On identical NaN-bearing input, raw_roi_mean, roi_minus_reference and spatial_z all return nan; glm_contrast_z alone returns a finite plausible number. The project's de facto NaN detector is failure-by-propagation in the other statistics, and this function is the single hole in it.

3. NARROW the failure narrative. The claimed corruption of scripts/detection_floor_table.py is not currently realizable and should not be asserted as an active harm: on the real simulation path (build_brain / clip_map, v3b design, 10 reps) there are no NaNs and the minimum se is 1.196e-02. No NaN is produced or handled anywhere in tribe_tools (clean grep over 8 files, exit 1). The correct framing is prospective: the exposure opens when MASTER-PLAN.md:392 runs glm_contrast_z on real TRIBE predictions in S2, plus the standing defect that the docstring states a guarantee the code does not honor.

Also minor: attenuation is not exactly k/58. Zeroing a vertex removes that vertex's own z from the sum, so k/58 holds only in expectation over vertices of equal effect. My run: 15.398 -> 12.336 on 5 vertices, where 4/5 * 15.398 = 12.318.

The proposed fix is sound in shape. Two refinements: the finiteness check should run on the ROI slices av/bv rather than the full arrays, so that NaN in an irrelevant vertex outside the ROI does not raise; and the relative degeneracy test should be scaled by the data magnitude rather than diff alone, e.g. compare se against eps * max(1.0, abs(av).max(), abs(bv).max()), since diff itself is near zero for a vertex that is constant in both conditions and would make the threshold vanish.

doctrine\\n|Two divergent MDE estimators.reasoning:
I re-derived every load-bearing part of this finding independently and it collapses. The surface facts are right; the consequence is wrong, and the proposed fix would corrupt the paper's single most important number.

WHAT IS TRUE (verified by reading, not by trusting the finding):
- /home/deveshb/workspace/AI/tribe-bench/scripts/detection_floor_table.py:31-37 does import `glm_contrast_z, perm_p, raw_roi_mean, roi_minus_reference, spatial_z` and NOT `detection_floor`. Confirmed.
- A scoped grep over tests/ scripts/ tribe_tools/ ops/ shows `detection_floor` is referenced only at tests/test_roi_stats.py:125/412-418, roi_stats.py:544, and two ops docs. It is called by nothing but its own test. `interpolate_floor` is referenced only inside detection_floor_table.py. Confirmed: the shipped floors come from an untested path.

WHY IT DOES NOT MATTER — THE TWO "ESTIMATORS" MEASURE DIFFERENT QUANTITIES:
`detection_floor(n, noise_sd, ...)` (roi_stats.py:544-613) knows nothing about any statistic. Its `achieved_power` draws `a ~ N(effect, noise_sd)`, `b ~ N(0, noise_sd)` and returns an MDE **in the units of whatever statistic you supplied the sd for**. The script's floors are in **raw predicted-response units** — an effect injected into the synthetic brain's FFCr columns and propagated through each statistic. Those coincide only when the statistic's gain w.r.t. the injected effect is 1.

I measured the gains (200 clips, /scratchpad/gain.py): d(raw_roi_mean)/d(effect) = 1.0000 exactly; d(spatial_z)/d(effect) = 3.034.

So I ran both estimators head to head (N_SIM=300, N_PERM=300, same synthetic brain, D_AUD=0.24, n=15, alpha=0.025):
  raw_roi_mean        detection_floor 0.0276  |  table-style 0.0298   (agree, ~7%, within grid+MC resolution)
  roi_minus_reference detection_floor 0.0195  |  table-style 0.0208   (agree, ~6%)
  spatial_z           detection_floor 0.1198 in z-units = **0.0395 raw**  |  table-style **0.1415 raw**  (3.6x disagreement)

The spatial_z gap is not noise — it is the retracted pathology itself. `detection_floor`'s shift model cannot represent a condition difference that moves the statistic's null centre (D_AUD=0.24 drags FACE-clip spatial_z down through the brain-wide normaliser). Adopting the finding's proposed fix would publish a spatial_z floor of ~0.04 instead of ~0.14 — 3.6x too optimistic, on the one number the paper says "makes the 2026-07-31 verdict uninterpretable". The finding's fix is the defect.

THE STATED FAILURE MODE IS BUILT ON A WRONG NUMBER:
The evidence says "N_SIM=100". The file says `N_SIM = 2000` (line 43); per-point SE at power 0.8 is 0.9%. Worse for the finding, `main()` re-seeds `rng = np.random.default_rng(20260820)` inside the effect loop and `face_effect` consumes no RNG — so every grid point runs the *identical* 2000 experiments with only an added constant. That is common random numbers, and it makes the curves monotone by construction. My run confirmed `monotone: True` for all three statistics across 13 grid points. "A single noisy grid point below target can push the reported floor higher" is not a live hazard here.

THE DOCSTRING CLAIM IS ALSO WEAKER THAN STATED:
roi_stats.py:438-439 says "the same one-sided permutation test the verdict uses". At n=15/15, comb(30,15)=155,117,520 > 20000, so `perm_p` routes to `mc_perm_p` — literally the same call `detection_floor` makes. For the three per-clip statistics the test is identical, not divergent. The unstated approximation is the *data model*, and the very next clause of the docstring already says "under additive Gaussian noise". glm_contrast_z is not a per-observation scalar so `detection_floor` was never applicable to it, and nothing tries.

Null calibration also checks out (power at effect 0: raw 0.023, rmr 0.013 vs alpha 0.025), so the untested path is empirically sound where I could reach it.

Net: no published number is corrupted, no silent wrong result is produced, and the untested estimator is the scientifically correct one — I independently reproduced its two commensurable floors with the tested function. Real but harmless as written, and actively harmful if "fixed" as proposed.

Measured here, using it for spatial_z would report a raw-unit floor of 0.0395 against the truth of 0.1415. For a compositional statistic (spatial_z, G020) it understates the floor — use the end-to-end injection simulation in scripts/detection_floor_table.py instead."
